components.label: External modules
components.plain: Packages maintained outside Cells could add laws and mechanisms that meet the same checks, accounting and execution contracts as the engine's own. Cells stays under the MIT licence, aiming at broad use (the user's direction, D180, 15 November 2026). Each part would be registered explicitly for one model build, then checked, assembled, compiled and run; registering a module that a model does not use changes nothing. The design note is still marked proposed. On 16 November 2026 the user, asking that others can easily add modules and laws by pull request, confirmed its five open decisions (D185). Contributed modules come first inside Cells, each in its own folder and namespace, under the MIT licence and with a named owner. A conformance kit shipped in Cells checks a module before its pull request; passing it means the kit's checks passed, not that the science is qualified. New physics still goes into the engine's source, as modules of its structure. The example module lives in this repository and is the template contributors copy. Development runs record an outside module's identity, and registered and judged runs also freeze its files. Two additions: the engine will write a declarations manifest, a list of every registered law, operator and kind with what it reads, writes and conserves, so that new modules appear in the documents and in this viewer's laws library without hand edits; and a contributor guide with a pull-request template. The four openings the design asked of the rework landed with it on 16 November 2026: kinds of piece are registered for one model build, exactly as an outside package would register them. Since 17 November 2026 laws and operators register the same way. Its first stage, one law from a separately installed package, is fifth in the plan's order after the landing, with the manifest and the guide. Since 17 November 2026 the import surface a module uses is on main, provisional, with no promise of stability until a first outside module arrives (D195), and the manifest is written (FR-12); since the evening of the same day the surface also exports the declaration types a family of its own needs: the law template, the family operator template and the record of a cited work; the kit, the example module and the guide come with the first stage. Still open: whether the project lists the modules that pass, and automatic checks on GitHub for outside pull requests.

components.label: Source layout by role
components.plain: The user decided on 16 November 2026 (D188) that the engine's source takes the modular layout: each law a module of its own, grouped by mechanism (channels, junctions, pumps, routes, reactions, transport), and folders of their own for kinds, operators, models, numerics, execution, the registry, definitions and records. The older model families move into a folder of legacy code that nothing outside it imports. It is reached by two scripted moves, the older families first, each checked at every commit: the same collected tests, the compiled programs unchanged, all 113 saved worlds the same, and tiers 1 and 2 with no changed outcome. Its first step is done: a read-only tool lists the families from the import graph, and on 16 November 2026 the user settled the list (D189). Nine families stay active, among them four that registered protocols name, whose shared code moves into the modular core; 102 become legacy. Its design note, proposed, and the two scripts that plan, make and check the moves have been on main since 17 November 2026. The note's probe ran the whole cycle on a scratch copy of the tree, never merged: a family moved, a coupled kernel taken out and moved, and every check came out identical. Five refactors came first, on 17 November 2026: the legacy entry point (R1), computed module paths named in full (R2), the parts of seven older modules that active code reaches taken verbatim into the core (R3), and two roots taken from the package instead of from a file's depth (R4, R5). The first move then landed on main the same day: the older families' 334 modules went into src/cells/legacy/ by its committed map, with no hand edits, keeping their sub-packages and their names, with no law, kind, operator or model identifier changed, and every gate held, a continuity resume across the move among them. Move 2, which puts the modular parts into the folders by role, is next, and no checkpoint crosses it (D195). First, as decided on 17 November 2026 (D198), the processes folder is dissolved as the first batch of removals: what an active entry point reaches moves, and the rest retires with its tests. That batch is held (D206): the user decided the same day that the physical laws in it are first carried onto seam F's law template, even those not used yet, each with one reference check against saved outputs of the old code and a visible not-qualified status, after a table that sorts its 33 modules and at a lower priority than the gap-junction replication; its numerical methods and geometry machinery wait for the engine's own geometry design. Later that evening the user decided that tested laws of the older code are ported to the active engine, the 54 law IDs behind 38 of the protein atlas's 48 units first, after a read-only inventory and one pilot family, below GARD and the gap-junction replication in priority; this amends D196, and the retire batch's two laws join it. Mechanisms already owned are not ported as they stand: calcium handling folds into the cardiac laws, mitochondria into their own design, and the junction flux into FR-16. A law that becomes declared is not thereby qualified (D211). The moves are the first step of the order the user set (D194). Files are moved, not rewritten: putting each law's declaration, mathematics and citation in one module is a separate pass. Planned: the first move is made, and the second is not.

components.label: Run-view output
components.plain: Every run can save what a viewer needs to replay it: geometry, identities, record metadata, events and how each layer is represented (D154). The writer merged into main on the evening of 16 November 2026, with its tests. A run that asks for it writes one view file beside its definition, through the shared output paths, and writing it changes no result. components.plain: The first living-cell loop, on main since the evening of 16 November 2026 with the run-view writer: a builder for the planarian's loop and one driver for every package. components.label: GPU-native execution
components.plain: What the rebuilt core already shows of the engine's GPU requirements. Since the rework landed on 16 November 2026, two hold, each shown by a test on main: a law that a world does not declare is absent from its compiled program, and a change of parameters alone reuses the compiled program and gives, bit for bit, what a fresh compile gives. Since the evening of the same day, a run of one world in windows can also check its saved rows on the device, on request: a second compiled program tests each window's rows, and any failure, or any account above half its bound, hands the window back to the usual checks on the host. This is opt-in and qualified on the CPU only. It is refused on a GPU until a GPU measurement exists, and for a world with an operator that retires cells, as division does, until a planted test exists. Every run made both ways gave the same results bit for bit, and no window was handed back. Against the host's checks on the same processors, the measured runs were 1.05 to 4.8 times as fast, and two long runs, whose host side is estimated, about 9 and 14 times. What is still to come on the GPU is a part of its own.

components.plain: What the rebuilt core must still show on a GPU. In production, stepping, step checks and refusals stay on the device, with no Python per cell and no CPU solver in the loop. components.label: Packed GPU execution
components.plain: Many worlds of one structure packed into one batch on the GPU, to keep it busy. On the L4, one world of the 825-node tissue keeps about a quarter of the GPU's processors active; 128 worlds or more keep about 90% active. The same planner is meant to serve production ensembles. Its design was proposed on 15 November 2026, at the user's request, and a planner is built on a branch of its own. In a development run on the L4 on 16 November 2026, packed repeats were identical bit for bit, but packing alone moved some small flux and ledger values by up to 1.6e-8 relative, more than the criterion set for it. The same day this was traced to rounding amplified by the conditioning of the field solve: the moved values are small differences of potentials. The direction ruled judges each field at 1e-12 of the scale it is computed from, with an empirical cap for the outside network's ledgers and an exact check of what the host computes from the state; it is not frozen until a held-out pass on the merged code. The four seams it asked of the core landed with the windows lane on the evening of 16 November 2026: arguments built for each window, a world named on every refusal, a typed refusal for memory, and an opt-in mode that sets a refused world aside and carries on with the others. The planner merges after its own gate, and its one-time GPU qualification runs on the merged code. Not on main.

components.label: One thread for linear algebra
components.plain: So that a run on ordinary processors gives the same bits however many processors it is given. The core found on 16 November 2026 that a run's bits followed the number of threads its linear-algebra libraries use, which follows the processors a run is given, and the user decided the same evening (D190) to run them on one thread. It merged into main just after midnight on 17 November 2026: every such library runs on one thread from the first import of the engine's core, and again at each of the eight places a run starts; the counts are read back, and a run is refused if any is not at one. Run manifests record each library's version, kernel and thread count, and checkpoints written before the pin still restore. With it, the 825-node world gives the same bits on 1, 2 and 4 processors. components.label: Scoped composition (door S)
components.plain: How several operators share one field. Before the rework, one operator supplied a field and replaced all of it, so two operators that touch different cells of the same field could not be combined. Since the rework landed on 16 November 2026, an operator can declare which cells or nodes it reads and changes, whether its change adds, multiplies or replaces, and at which stage of the step; the composite model then merges the changes place by place. Two operators that change separate places must give the same result in either order, and an overlap is refused unless a rule says how to combine it. Tests on main show its acceptance: two operators on separate places give the same bits in either order, and an overlap is refused unless both changes commute. In the round, operators that close cells still change whole masks, and the one pair newly admitted is the scheduled bath beside the shared-inventory reactions; the other pairs keep their refusals. components.label: Test tiers gate
components.plain: The routine gate: every test file's outcome is compared with a recorded baseline before code lands. A file counts as changed when its exit code or its count of failures or errors differs, when its count of passing tests falls, or when its count of skipped tests rises. At D172's landing on 16 November 2026, tiers 1 and 2 (492 files) showed no changed outcome. Of tier 3's 229 files, 187 passed, and each of the other 42 was classified, none of them a defect of the round: 23 failures and 16 time-outs that were there before, two tests the round left stale, fixed in the next commit, and one that passes when run alone. The user's rule of the same day (D187) is to test as little as possible but enough for the science: each claim is proved once, at the cheapest level that can prove it, a new test must catch a planted error, and each landing's tier-3 table is frozen as the record the next run is compared with. The audit's tools merged on the evening of 16 November 2026: tier 3's table is frozen test by test, so that a later run of tier 3 is compared test by test instead of running old code again. The user approved the audit's firm list of tests to retire the same evening (D189), and the retire merged early on 17 November 2026: 11 whole files of tier 3 and 40 of tiers 1 and 2 were deleted, and 811 cases were removed from 42 more, while eight rows were held instead, each with its reason. The tiers now hold 327, 152 and 222 files, and tier 3's frozen record holds 218 files and 6,869 tests. The saving is 5.5 processor-hours per run of tier 3 and 2 minutes per gate of tiers 1 and 2. The tree before the retire is tagged, so that every retired test stays recoverable.
